content: The Eastern tiger swallowtail, scientifically known as Papilio glaucus, is a large butterfly with a wingspan of approximately 12 cm. It is native to the Eastern United States, ranging as far north as southern Vermont and extending westward to the easternmost parts of Colorado. This butterfly is active from spring through fall, and in the southern regions of its range, it can produce two or three broods annually. In the Appalachian region, the Eastern tiger swallowtail is replaced by a closely related species, Papilio appalachiensis, which was only recently described. In the northern parts of its range, it is replaced by another closely related species, Papilio canadensis. These three species are morphologically similar and were historically considered a single species, making them difficult to distinguish. Adult male Eastern tiger swallowtails are yellow with four distinct black tiger stripes on each forewing. The trailing edges of both the forewings and hindwings are black, interrupted by yellow spots. On the medial margin of the hindwings, near the abdomen, there are small red and blue spots. Adult females exhibit two distinct morphs: a yellow morph and a dark morph. The yellow morph resembles the male but features a blue area on the hindwings between the black margin and the main yellow region. In the dark morph, most of the yellow areas are replaced by dark gray to black, though faint tiger stripes are still visible. The dark morph is more prevalent in the southern parts of the range, particularly in areas also inhabited by the Pipevine Swallowtail (Battus philenor), which it appears to mimic. Eastern tiger swallowtails often rest with their wings fully spread, especially in sunny conditions. Females lay spherical green eggs on the upper surfaces of host plant leaves. After hatching, the caterpillars frequently consume the eggshell. The early instar caterpillars are dark in color and mimic bird droppings as a form of camouflage. The larvae feed on the leaves of a wide variety of trees and shrubs, including cottonwood, tulip tree, sweet bay, and cherry. Adult butterflies are strictly diurnal, beginning their flight activity around noon and returning to rest during the afternoon. This behavior has been documented in studies such as those by Fullard and Napoleone (2001). The Eastern tiger swallowtail holds the distinction of being the state butterfly of Georgia, Virginia, Alabama, South Carolina, and Delaware.
